doc.title: Joe Ascione interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Making a reputation by word of mouth; Hofstra and staying in New York
summary: Ascione says reputation comes from good musical experiences and word of mouth. On Charlie Perry's advice he chose Hofstra and stayed in New York, mixing street and school routes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Great, man. How do you go about making your reputation in today’s jazz world?

I think ultimately the musical playing experience is the musician’s greatest asset. So more often than not people I’ve had the opportunity to play with have been people that, either through recommendation and then a great musical experience would occur, and then from there word spreads. It’s more word of mouth. There is no school for something like that. Occasionally it’s through the distant recommendation, but more often than not from a good musical experience I’ll get a return call or through that word of mouth promoter or tour director or record date, fellow musician. That’s the greatest tool.
A lot of the guys are going the jazz college route these days.

I aspired to do that. I had several scholarships to a few of the top places. I ultimately stayed in New York, Long Island proper, at Hofstra University. They had a pretty good jazz program. The reason being, I was studying with Charlie Perry in the 70s and he said, “What do you want to do?” I said, “I want to play my drums.” He said, “Stay in New York. If you go to college good for you, it’ll be a positive thing.” He said, “If you go away there’s one philosophy you can come back four years later and say ‘here’s my paper’ and yay, or,” he said, “why don’t you stay here and start playing and develop the craft and go that route.” So I did. I think of myself taking the middle of the road. No, it’s an intermediate road. Some players just came up through the school of the street and that was it. Other players came the route of the college and getting picked up by a big band, let’s say the Buddy Rich Big Band or Woody Herman or whomever, or forming groups © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

themselves. I sort of have taken the route of both of them. I’m street wise and gig chops experienced and yet I have the school background also. But I stayed in New York predominantly through that period.
